Chapter Four: The Surveyor's Return

The valley had changed little in twenty years. Owen walked the last mile along the cart track with his coat over his arm, counting the same stone walls, the same gates, the same row of poplars that leaned toward the water. The river was low. The mill stood where it had always stood, its wheel fixed and green with moss, and the yard behind it was quiet. He stopped at the bridge and looked at the house on the far bank. The shutters were open. A woman was shaking a cloth from the upper window, and a dog slept in the sun by the door.

He had come back to measure the land again, as his father had done before him and as the office in the county town still required every generation or so. The instruments were in the case on his shoulder: a level, a staff, a chain of brass links, and a notebook with ruled pages that had never been used. He set the case down on the parapet and took out the notebook, and for a while he wrote nothing at all.

The village had kept its habits. The baker opened at five and closed at noon. The school bell rang at nine and at three, and the children came out shouting into the lane and drifted home in twos and threes. The post came on Tuesdays. In the evenings the older men sat on the bench outside the inn and talked about the weather, about the price of hay, about a cousin who had gone to the city and had not written since. They talked slowly and at length, and no one hurried them.

It was market day when he finally went down to the square. The stalls were set out in two long rows, and the square was full of people standing shoulder to shoulder, waiting for the auction to begin. Owen stood at the edge of the crowd and listened. The auctioneer called the lots one after another, and the bidding rose and fell, and the morning went by. The light had turned utterly grey by the time the last lot was sold, and the square emptied slowly, and the women carried their baskets home.

The rain came on in the afternoon and the road turned to mud. He walked back up the hill with the case on his shoulder, and by the time he reached the bridge his boots were completely soaked and the notebook in his pocket was damp at the corners. The river had risen a little. A heron stood in the shallows below the weir, and the water carried leaves past it, and the leaves turned and sank and came up again further down.

He climbed to the ridge above the mill, where the old boundary stone still marked the parish line, and he set up the level and read the staff and wrote the figures in the damp pages. The wind was cold. The clouds moved eastwards in long grey ranks, and the poplars bent and straightened and bent again. He packed the instruments away, and he sat on the stone for a while with his hands in his pockets, and he watched the valley fill with shadows until he could no longer tell the hedges from the fields.

There was nothing more to measure that day. He went down to the inn, where a fire was burning and the same bench stood outside the door, and he ate bread and cheese and drank a glass of beer and listened to the men talk about the weather. Later he climbed the stairs to a room with a low ceiling and a narrow bed, and he slept, and in the morning he walked back to the county town and filed the figures in the office, and the work was done.
